what_its_for: Mesna is a protective medicine given to prevent a serious bladder problem called hemorrhagic cystitis (bleeding in the bladder) that can be caused by certain chemotherapy drugs, especially ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide. It works by neutralizing harmful byproducts of these chemotherapy medicines before they can irritate or damage the lining of your bladder.
how_to_take: Mesna can be given in two ways: as an injection into your vein (IV) through a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting, or as tablets taken by mouth. If you are taking the tablets at home, swallow them whole with a full glass of water. It is very important to drink plenty of fluids (at least 6 to 8 glasses of water or juice) throughout the day while you are receiving this medicine. Try to urinate frequently to help flush your bladder. Take mesna exactly as prescribed — it is usually given at specific times around your chemotherapy treatment, so follow your schedule carefully.
dosing: Your dose of mesna is carefully calculated by your doctor based on the dose of chemotherapy you are receiving. It is typically given at 0, 4, and 8 hours after your chemotherapy dose, but your schedule may vary. Do not change your dose or timing without talking to your doctor first. If you are taking oral tablets at home, make sure you understand exactly when to take each dose before you leave the clinic.
missed_dose: Because mesna works on a very specific time schedule to protect your bladder, it is very important not to miss a dose. If you miss a dose of the oral tablets at home, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is within 2 hours of the scheduled time. If it has been more than 2 hours, skip that missed dose and call your doctor or nurse right away for instructions. Do not double up on doses to make up for a missed one. If you vomit within 2 hours of taking a tablet, contact your doctor or nurse immediately, as you may need a replacement dose.
storage: Store mesna tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. If you are given mesna as a liquid solution to take at home, ask your pharmacist or nurse for specific storage instructions, as it may need to be refrigerated and used within a certain time frame.
what_to_avoid: Do not skip doses of mesna or change your dosing schedule without talking to your doctor. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of water and fluids throughout your treatment day. Avoid alcohol during your cancer treatment unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as some may interact with mesna or your chemotherapy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you notice any of the following: blood in your urine (urine looks pink, red, or cola-colored), pain or burning when you urinate, feeling like you need to urinate frequently or urgently, little or no urine output, severe stomach or lower belly pain, signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of your face or throat, difficulty breathing, or a sudden drop in blood pressure. Also call your doctor if you are vomiting and unable to keep your mesna tablets down, or if you have any unusual or concerning symptoms.
when_it_works: Mesna begins working very quickly after it is given. It is designed to be active in your bladder at the same time the harmful chemotherapy byproducts arrive there. This is why timing is so important. You may not notice any direct effects from mesna itself — that is normal. Its job is to work quietly in the background to keep your bladder safe. Most people are able to complete their chemotherapy without bladder problems when mesna is used correctly.
special_populations: Older adults may need extra monitoring for side effects. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, tell your doctor before starting treatment, as both mesna and the chemotherapy medicines it is used with can affect pregnancy. It is not known if mesna passes into breast milk, so breastfeeding is generally not recommended during cancer chemotherapy — discuss this with your doctor. If you have kidney or liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your treatment plan. Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions before starting mesna.
